heading_path: WS-POL-C  –  Scope, Triaging, and Policy Crosswalk
sections.text: I do not think FCCPS should write an AI policy that is so narrow it governs only the most obvious current controversies, nor so broad that it becomes an unadministrable theory of all technology risk. The right approach is a broad but disciplined scope. FCCPS should write this policy to cover AI uses that materially affect student learning, assessment validity, student rights, student well-being, privacy, equity, or district governance. That means the policy should certainly address generative AI and detectors, because those are the most visible and immediate issues. But it should not stop there. It should also be capable of reaching AI-enabled systems, tools, and workflows used in FCCPS contexts when they change the practical risk environment enough that ordinary existing policy language is no longer sufficient. That is the key threshold: not whether a tool is branded “AI,” but whether AI changes scale, ambiguity, evidentiary conditions, or implementation burden in ways the Board should govern explicitly.

heading_path: WS-POL-C  –  Scope, Triaging, and Policy Crosswalk
sections.text: In my view, a GenAI-only frame is too narrow for the policy itself, even if GenAI remains the center of gravity in communications and examples. The district will confront not only chatbots and generators, but also AI-enabled screening, translation, personalization, workflow, monitoring, and decision-support systems. Some of those tools will not present as “ChatGPT for school,” yet may have greater consequences for students and staff than classroom prompting alone. FCCPS should therefore write the policy so that it applies more broadly to AI-enabled systems used in FCCPS contexts, while using guidance and examples to keep the document concrete and understandable. This lets the Board avoid writing a policy that is obsolete the moment the product category shifts, while still acknowledging that generative AI is the current focal point of community concern.

heading_path: WS-POL-C  –  Scope, Triaging, and Policy Crosswalk
sections.text: I also think this section should say plainly that academic integrity is not the only AI policy problem. Integrity matters, but it is not sufficient as the organizing scope of the policy. FCCPS should explicitly recognize non-academic AI risks where they materially affect the school environment, especially manipulative interaction, quasi-social dependence, harassment, synthetic media abuse, inappropriate content exposure, and contexts in which students may be nudged away from human support or judgment. I am not suggesting that this report attempt to solve every such issue in detail. I am saying the Board should be told that these risks belong within the district’s AI policy perimeter and should not be treated as accidental side effects outside the policy’s concern. If the committee omits them from Section C, the policy shell will understate the real problem FCCPS is trying to govern.

heading_path: WS-POL-C  –  Scope, Triaging, and Policy Crosswalk
sections.text: At the same time, I would not write this section as an invitation to policy sprawl. The policy should not attempt to prescribe a separate rule for every conceivable AI-enabled feature or classroom edge case. Instead, FCCPS should adopt a triage structure. In my judgment, the district needs a practical way to sort AI uses by risk, consequence, and context. The policy should establish that not all AI uses are alike and that different uses warrant different levels of scrutiny, restriction, disclosure, or approval. A low-risk assistive use that does not touch student records or displace core learning work should not be governed in the same way as an identity-linked system, a detector, a student-facing conversational tool, or an AI-supported process affecting discipline, placement, accommodations, or other consequential decisions.

heading_path: WS-POL-C  –  Scope, Triaging, and Policy Crosswalk
sections.text: I therefore support a triaging approach that asks at least four questions. First, what is the educational or operational function of the AI use? Second, what is the risk level, including privacy, fairness, developmental, and well-being risk? Third, who is affected and in what context, including grade band and vulnerability of the user population? Fourth, does the use alter a decision or workflow that already carries heightened legal, ethical, or trust implications? Those questions are more durable than a policy built around product labels alone. They allow FCCPS to remain flexible as technologies evolve while still giving administrators and educators a usable structure for judgment.

heading_path: WS-POL-C  –  Scope, Triaging, and Policy Crosswalk
sections.text: I would also distinguish here between policy-level triage and implementation-level triage. At the policy level, the Board should state that uses may be categorized and treated differently based on risk, consequence, and developmental appropriateness. At the implementation level, the district can then build the supporting matrices, tool-review criteria, examples, and approval pathways. That distinction matters because I do not think the Board-facing report should be overloaded with operational detail. But I do think the Board should be told that triage is a core design principle of the policy, not a back-office administrative preference.

heading_path: WS-POL-C  –  Scope, Triaging, and Policy Crosswalk
sections.text: On the relationship to existing FCCPS policy and regulation, I support an overlay model, not a replacement model. FCCPS does not need a single AI policy that tries to supersede academic integrity rules, student conduct standards, privacy practices, vendor review, bullying and harassment protections, discipline procedures, accessibility obligations, and staff guidance all at once. It needs an AI policy that works alongside those frameworks and clarifies where AI changes the problem. In some areas, existing policy may already govern the underlying conduct, and AI mainly changes evidence, scale, speed, or enforceability. In other areas, AI may introduce enough novelty or ambiguity that additional guidance is needed. Section C should say that explicitly and should recommend a formal appendix or crosswalk identifying where existing FCCPS policies already apply, where clarification is needed, and where future revision should be considered.

heading_path: WS-POL-C  –  Scope, Triaging, and Policy Crosswalk
sections.text: In practical terms, I would have the crosswalk do three things. First, identify existing policy areas that already govern conduct or obligations implicated by AI. Second, identify where AI creates a meaningful change in implementation burden, evidentiary uncertainty, or governance risk. Third, identify where AI-specific guidance, regulation, procurement standards, or administrative procedures need to be layered on top. That is a better approach than pretending the Board can resolve every operational dependency in one policy section. It is also more honest about the district’s actual policy architecture.

heading_path: WS-POL-C  –  Scope, Triaging, and Policy Crosswalk
sections.text: My own position, then, is that WS-POL-C should recommend a policy scope that is challenge-based, governance-aware, and future-resilient. FCCPS should not write this section as though the only live issue is whether students use ChatGPT on essays. Nor should it write the section so expansively that no one can tell what falls inside the policy. The right middle path is to say: the policy applies where AI materially affects learning, assessment, rights, well-being, privacy, equity, or governance; uses should be triaged according to risk and consequence; and AI-specific guidance should be cross-walked to existing FCCPS policy rather than treated as a freestanding replacement for the district’s broader rules.

heading_path: WS-POL-C  –  Scope, Triaging, and Policy Crosswalk
sections.text: That, in my view, is the most defensible way to write Section C. It is broad enough to govern the real problem, narrow enough to remain usable, and structured enough to support later guidance, procurement, communications, and implementation work without forcing the Board-facing document to do all of that work itself.

title: WS-POL-C  –  Scope, Triaging, and Policy Crosswalk
